prompt: In Bento's first week he asks whether a seat stays held when the payment gateway is slow. Why can the printout on the wall not answer him?

choices.text: It shows the gateway's logo but no other part of the purchase
choices.why: The printout has the gateway's logo and arrows touching it; what it lacks is something else.

choices.text: Its picture has no time in it
choices.why: Right: the question is about what happens while a call waits, and the picture has no time in it.

choices.text: Its arrows point from the database to the phone
choices.why: The direction of its arrows is not why it fails here.

choices.text: It was drawn in UML, which Bento has not learnt
choices.why: The printout is logos and arrows, not UML.

prompt: A container diagram colours some services green and others blue, with no key beside it. What does the lesson expect a reader to do with the colours?

choices.text: Read past them, since colour on a diagram is decoration
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: colour is a strong signal and readers try to decode it.

choices.text: Assume the green services are the newer ones
choices.why: That is one guess among many; the point is what readers do in general.

choices.text: Decode them into a meaning nobody intended
choices.why: Right: colour is a strong signal, so either a legend says what it means or the diagram uses one colour.

choices.text: Ask the author before reading on
choices.why: The reader of a handed-over diagram has nobody to ask, which is why the legend exists.

prompt: Tainá draws a dashed box around the ticketing API, the booking database and the seat-hold store, and writes nothing on it. What should she change?

choices.text: Make it a solid line, so it reads as a firm claim
choices.why: The line style is not the problem; the missing name is.

choices.text: Name the boundary, and keep one kind of boundary on the diagram
choices.why: Right: deployed together, owned by one team, inside our network and one bounded context are four different claims.

choices.text: Delete it, because a boundary belongs on a deployment diagram instead
choices.why: Boundaries appear on many kinds of diagram; they need a name, not a different picture.

choices.text: Draw the three boxes the same size
choices.why: Size is its own claim, and it does not say what the box around them means.

prompt: Rui wants to know what runs on which machine and how the machines are connected. Which of Kruchten's views answers him?

choices.text: The logical view
choices.why: That one is about the main abstractions and how they relate, for designers.

choices.text: The development view, about modules and owners
choices.why: That one is about how the code is organised and who owns which part.

choices.text: The process view, about what runs at the same time
choices.why: That one is about concurrency and how the running parts communicate.

choices.text: The physical view
choices.why: Right: machines and networks, for operations and platform, drawn as a deployment diagram.

prompt: When Bento explains Tainá's purchase diagram back to her, he reads the arrow to the payment gateway as the gateway calling Carcará back when a payment clears. What did the fix look like?

choices.text: Reverse that arrow, so it points from the gateway to the API
choices.why: The original call is still real; turning it round would lose it.

choices.text: Walk Bento through the diagram before he reads it
choices.why: Explaining it first is exactly what the test forbids, since later readers will not get the walk-through.

choices.text: A second, dashed line the other way, labelled as the webhook, and a legend entry for dashed lines
choices.why: Right: the callback was real and missing, so it got its own labelled line and a key.

choices.text: Move the gateway to a sequence diagram of its own
choices.why: The defect was a missing claim on this diagram, not the wrong kind of picture.

prompt: An architecture document shows two boxes and one arrow: the ticketing API writes to the booking database. Which of the four things a picture carries does this one carry?

choices.text: A sequence in time, because the write follows the request
choices.why: One arrow holds no chain of steps that depend on each other.

choices.text: A count, because it shows two elements
choices.why: A count is many things at once, which prose merely asserts, such as 300 phones syncing.

choices.text: A nesting, because the database sits behind the API
choices.why: No box is drawn inside another, and no line crosses a boundary.

choices.text: It carries no more than the sentence it restates
choices.why: Right: drawn, it is two boxes the reader decodes back into the same sentence, at the same upkeep.

prompt: Put the parts of a readable diagram in the order the lesson says a reader looks for them.
items: A title that says what is shown and at what scope
A type on every element
A label on every line
A legend for every kind of mark
A date or a version, and an owner
trap: The title comes first because it says what the rest is about; the date is the last check, on whether it is still true.

prompt: On Carcará's use case diagram, a station agent can do everything a passenger can, at a counter, and more. How is that drawn?

choices.text: An «extend» arrow drawn from the passenger to the station agent
choices.why: Extend joins two use cases, for optional behaviour; it does not join actors.

choices.text: A hollow-headed arrow from the station agent to the passenger
choices.why: Right: actors are generalised with a hollow-headed arrow pointing at the more general one.

choices.text: An «include» arrow between the two actors
choices.why: Include is for a step shared between use cases.

choices.text: A boundary drawn around both of them
choices.why: Actors stay outside the system boundary.

prompt: On the booking class diagram, a dashed line with an open arrowhead runs from Booking to PricingPolicy. What does it claim?

choices.text: Each booking owns a policy, deleted with it
choices.why: That would be composition, a solid line with a filled diamond.

choices.text: Booking asks the policy for a fare and keeps no link to it afterwards
choices.why: Right: a dependency is a use, such as a parameter, without a held reference.

choices.text: Booking holds a reference to one pricing policy for its whole lifetime
choices.why: A held link is an association, drawn solid.

choices.text: PricingPolicy implements an interface that Booking defines for its fares
choices.why: Realisation has a hollow triangle, pointing at the interface.

prompt: Each ticket has an arrowhead pointing at its trip, and a trip holds no list of its tickets. Why does the lesson call that direction a decision that matters?

choices.text: Trips are shared by the passengers on the bus
choices.why: True of trips, but it is not the reason the lesson gives for the arrowhead.

choices.text: The busiest trip has 44 seats and some 400 dead tickets behind them
choices.why: Right: about four hundred cancelled or expired tickets would hang off a trip that carried the list.

choices.text: A trip would be deleted together with the last ticket pointing at it
choices.why: A trip outlives the tickets that point at it.

choices.text: UML forbids arrowheads at both ends
choices.why: Both ends are allowed; the lesson's point is that each arrowhead should be a decision.

prompt: In the purchase sequence, the declined branch sends release seat to the seat-hold store with an open arrowhead. What does that arrowhead say?

choices.text: The message is a reply to an earlier call
choices.why: A reply is a dashed line with an open arrowhead.

choices.text: The store answers with the reason for the decline
choices.why: The reason goes to the app, and the arrowhead does not describe an answer.

choices.text: The API does not wait for the store
choices.why: Right: an open arrowhead is an asynchronous message, and the sender carries on.

choices.text: The release runs in parallel with the payment, inside a par fragment
choices.why: No par fragment is drawn; the release happens after the decline.

prompt: A draft deployment diagram draws Pricing as a 3D box, though Pricing is a module inside the ticketing service. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: It claims Pricing is a separate machine
choices.why: Right: a node is something that runs software; a module belongs inside the artifact, or on the component diagram.

choices.text: Each node needs the keyword «device»
choices.why: Execution environments are nodes too, with their own keyword.

choices.text: Modules are drawn as lifelines on deployment diagrams
choices.why: Lifelines belong to sequence diagrams.

choices.text: In UML, a 3D box stands for a person using the system
choices.why: A person in UML is an actor, a stick figure.

prompt: From Carcará's p95 times — 120 ms to the API, 1,400 ms for the card charge, 8 ms for the database write and 120 ms back — how many milliseconds of the chain are NOT the gateway's charge?
Drawing search trips, then choose seat, then pay as arrows on a use case diagram is wrong because a use case diagram has no ___ in it.
On the system context diagram, which label suits the line from Carcará ticketing to the payment gateway?

choices.text: HTTPS/JSON
choices.why: A context diagram is for everybody, and a protocol means little to most of them.

choices.text: uses
choices.why: It fits any arrow, so it carries no meaning.

choices.text: charges cards and Pix through
choices.why: Right: it says what is done, from the perspective of the arrow's source.

choices.text: REST over the internet, through the load balancer
choices.why: That mixes protocol and infrastructure into a picture meant for everybody.

prompt: The passenger web app and the mobile app both talk to the same ticketing API. Why are they two containers?

choices.text: They are built, released and run separately
choices.why: Right: a container is a runtime boundary, and these two are deployed on their own.

choices.text: They are written in different languages, TypeScript against Kotlin and Swift
choices.why: The technology differs, but the reason is that each one runs and ships separately.

choices.text: They are owned by two different teams
choices.why: Sales builds both; ownership is a boundary, not what makes a container.

choices.text: C4 draws one container per screen of the app
choices.why: A container is a separately running thing, not a screen.

prompt: On Carcará's container diagram, seat holds sit in Redis and bookings in PostgreSQL. What reason does the lesson give for two stores?

choices.text: A hold is temporary and hot; a booking is permanent
choices.why: Right: two kinds of data, with two different demands, in two stores.

choices.text: PostgreSQL was too slow to store anything for the purchase
choices.why: Bookings live in PostgreSQL, so that is not the reason.

choices.text: Platform already ran Redis for sessions and wanted to reuse it
choices.why: That was one force in the later record, not the container diagram's reason.

choices.text: Each team gets its own store
choices.why: The stores are split by the kind of data, not by team.

prompt: The boarding app talks to a boarding sync service rather than to the ticketing API. What does the sync give the app?

choices.text: A live check of each ticket against the booking database
choices.why: A live check needs signal, which the road frequently lacks.

choices.text: Each bus's ticket list before departure, and a place to upload scans once it has signal
choices.why: Right: that is what lets boarding work on a road with no signal.

choices.text: Payment confirmations from the gateway
choices.why: Those reach the ticketing API's webhook handler.

choices.text: The next day's trips from Frota
choices.why: Frota sends trips to the ticketing API.

prompt: The container diagram has an arrow from the mobile app to the ticketing API. On the API's component diagram, no component receives anything from the app. What does the lesson say is broken?

choices.text: The component diagram should leave the outside containers off it
choices.why: Outside containers appear wherever a component talks to them; that is how the levels stay consistent.

choices.text: The mobile app should be drawn as a component
choices.why: The app runs on its own, so it is a container.

choices.text: A relationship at one level has to be explained by relationships at the level below
choices.why: Right: here it has been lost on the way down, and the controllers that receive it are missing.

choices.text: A dynamic diagram is needed instead
choices.why: A dynamic diagram tells a story; it does not mend a missing element.

prompt: Put the numbered steps of the dynamic diagram of the purchase in order, after the app creates the booking.
items: The API holds the seat in the seat-hold store
The API writes the pending booking to the booking database
The API charges the payment gateway
The API marks the booking paid
The API publishes ticket sold to the broker
The notification worker sends the ticket
trap: The seat is held and the booking written before any money moves; the ticket is sent last, by the worker, after the event is published.

prompt: Which of these belong on a C4 deployment diagram rather than on the container diagram? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The load balancer in front of the API
choices.why: Right: infrastructure is where containers run, not a container.

choices.text: Three replicas of the ticketing API
choices.why: Right: replicas and counts are deployment facts; the container is drawn once.

choices.text: The cloud region the cluster runs in
choices.why: Right: regions are deployment nodes.

choices.text: What the ticketing API does for the passenger app
choices.why: That is the relationship's description, which the container diagram carries.

prompt: A draft activity diagram of the cancellation has lanes named Cloud region, Bus station and Bus. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Lanes are for who performs each step: a role, a team or a system
choices.why: Right: lanes answer whose step it is, not where it happens.

choices.text: Add a fourth lane for the payment gateway's own data centre as well
choices.why: That is one more lane about place, which is the problem.

choices.text: Swap the lanes for BPMN pools, one per place
choices.why: A pool is a participant organisation, not a location.

choices.text: Keep them, since lanes show where each step runs
choices.why: The lesson says lanes are for who, not for where.

prompt: A refund process crosses to the payment company, Joana's analysts will maintain the model, and a process engine may run it later. Which notation does the lesson point to?

choices.text: A classic flowchart
choices.why: That suits a short procedure for a non-technical reader, without parallelism.

choices.text: A UML activity diagram, alongside the other UML
choices.why: That fits a software design document; this process crosses organisations.

choices.text: A state machine of the refund
choices.why: A state machine follows one object, not a process between organisations.

choices.text: BPMN
choices.why: Right: those are the three cases the lesson gives for BPMN.

prompt: A reviewer finds the state Sending e-mail in a draft machine for a ticket. Which check does the lesson give to settle whether it belongs?

choices.text: Whether you could query the database and find it there tomorrow morning
choices.why: Right: Paid passes that test; Sending e-mail lasts milliseconds and fails it.

choices.text: Whether the state has an entry action
choices.why: Entry actions are allowed on real states; they do not tell you whether this is one.

choices.text: Whether its name is a verb or a noun
choices.why: Naming is a clue, but the lesson's test is about what a query finds later.

choices.text: Whether the happy path passes through it
choices.why: The happy path is the part everybody already knows; it settles no question here.

prompt: A driver's phone loses signal and later resends its upload of a scan for a ticket already in Boarded. What does the state table decide for that resend?

choices.text: Refuse it as already used
choices.why: That is the answer at the door, when a second passenger shows the same ticket.

choices.text: Ignore it
choices.why: Right: a repeated event from the same phone changes no state, so it is ignored.

choices.text: Move the ticket to No-show
choices.why: No-show is for a ticket departed without being scanned.

choices.text: Raise an error and alert Payments
choices.why: A resend is ordinary, since phones resend when the signal drops.

prompt: Carcará's state table has six states and six events. How many cells does it have, each one asking what that event does in that state?
The payment gateway is upstream of Carcará even though Carcará calls it: upstream is about whose ___ wins, not about who opens the connection.
Match each line of Carcará's context map to the relationship it carries.

pairs.right: Sales translates Frota's model through an anticorruption layer
Boarding conforms to a published language

prompt: Bento wants a record for every library upgrade. Why does the lesson resist that?

choices.text: Records are kept for decisions made by the architects, not by the engineers
choices.why: The test is about cost of reversal and reach, not about who decided.

choices.text: A log of two hundred records about library versions is a log nobody reads
choices.why: Right: a record is for what is expensive to reverse and affects more than its authors.

choices.text: Library versions belong in a separate design document
choices.why: A design document explores; it is not where upgrades are tracked either.

choices.text: A record takes a week to write
choices.why: Most of Carcará's records are one page.

prompt: A draft context reads: after discussing it, the team felt the current approach was not working. What should replace it?

choices.text: A longer account of who said what in the meeting
choices.why: That makes the story longer, and the story is what was weak.

choices.text: The chosen option, stated early so the reader knows where it goes
choices.why: Stating the answer in the context is the solution in disguise.

choices.text: A list of facts, constraints and pressures somebody could check
choices.why: Right: forces, with numbers, such as 85% CPU at peak in June 2025.

choices.text: A link to the meeting notes
choices.why: Links support the context; they do not replace it.

prompt: Carcará's payment company was fixed by ADR-0003, and a later record depends on it. How should the later record handle its options?

choices.text: Add two alternatives so the record looks balanced
choices.why: A record that pretends to have options it did not weigh is the one the lesson rejects.

choices.text: Skip the record, as there was no real choice to make
choices.why: The later decision still deserves its record; it simply has one option.

choices.text: Leave the options section blank without comment
choices.why: The reader is then left guessing why.

choices.text: Say there was one option and link to what fixed it
choices.why: Right: for example, we use the payment company chosen in ADR-0003; no other was considered.

prompt: A consequence reads: this will make the system more scalable. What does the lesson call it?

choices.text: A wish with no measure
choices.why: Right: it should say what will scale, to what, and how anybody would know.

choices.text: A neutral consequence that creates new work
choices.why: Neutral consequences name concrete work, such as adding Redis to the runbook.

choices.text: A restatement of the decision
choices.why: Restating is writing we will use Redis as a consequence of choosing Redis.

choices.text: An implementation step that belongs in a ticket
choices.why: Steps are things like add a feature flag; this names no step.

prompt: Inside the Sales team, a choice is reversible within a sprint and still worth remembering. Which weight of record does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: A full record in the architecture repository
choices.why: That weight is for decisions that cross teams and are hard to reverse.

choices.text: A comment beside the function
choices.why: That is for a decision about one function.

choices.text: A Y-statement, or a row in a decision table
choices.why: Right: the reasoning is kept without the ceremony of a full record.

choices.text: Skip it, because it is easy to undo
choices.why: An unrecorded decision is decided by whoever touches the code next.

prompt: At peak, Carcará created 1,800 seat holds a minute and 70% of them expired without payment. How many holds a minute did not expire?
Put the five parts of a Nygard-style record in the order they appear on the page.
items: Title
Status
Context
Decision
Consequences
trap: The title and status tell a reader what was decided and whether it still applies before they read why.

prompt: Otávio asks for the ticket e-mail to show the bus company's logo. Is that architecturally significant?

choices.text: Yes, because a passenger sees each ticket e-mail
choices.why: Visibility is not the test; structure is.

choices.text: No: it changes a template, not the structure
choices.why: Right: significant means meeting it would change where data lives, what talks to what or what runs where.

choices.text: Yes, because it is a functional requirement
choices.why: Functional requirements shape what the system contains; most do not change the structure.

choices.text: No, because Otávio is not an engineer
choices.why: Who asks is not the test.

prompt: Walking ISO/IEC 25010 found interaction capability, which nobody had written. What made it matter at Carcará?

choices.text: The standard's 2023 revision renamed usability as interaction capability
choices.why: The rename is a fact about the standard, not a reason it matters here.

choices.text: A third of the drivers have low vision
choices.why: The lesson gives no such figure.

choices.text: 30% of ticket sales happen on phones more than five years old
choices.why: Right: a slow phone is a real buyer, and the checklist brought that up.

choices.text: The board had asked Tainá for an accessibility audit of the app
choices.why: No audit is mentioned; the finding came from walking the list.

prompt: The team first dismissed safety, then kept it for one case. Which?

choices.text: Drivers are not to read the phone while driving
choices.why: The lesson does not give that case.

choices.text: A cancelled ticket is refused at the door within a minute
choices.why: That is a quality requirement about freshness, traded against offline boarding.

choices.text: The app refuses a scan once the bus is full, whatever the list says
choices.why: Right: a driver is not to be pressed into boarding more passengers than seats.

choices.text: Refunds over R$ 500 are traceable to a person
choices.why: That is QS-05, a security scenario.

prompt: QS-01 asks that 95% of purchases complete within 2 seconds. What does the percentile say that an average would hide?

choices.text: How fast the payment gateway is
choices.why: QS-01 deliberately leaves the gateway's time out.

choices.text: The share of purchases allowed to be slow
choices.why: Right: the measure has a number and a scope, and an average hides the slow tail.

choices.text: Which tactic the design will use
choices.why: A scenario says what, not how.

choices.text: How many purchases start each minute at peak
choices.why: That is the environment, 2,000 a minute, not what the percentile adds.

prompt: Offline boarding uses local fallback, and its cost is staleness: a ticket sold after the last sync is not on the phone's list. What does the design add for that case?

choices.text: A sync each five minutes, so the list stays fresh
choices.why: Celeste chose fifteen minutes and accepted the staleness.

choices.text: Refuse each ticket the phone does not know
choices.why: That would turn away passengers who bought late and paid.

choices.text: An online check when signal exists; without it, the driver accepts a ticket shown with its purchase e-mail and the scan is checked later
choices.why: Right: a second tactic for the case the first one leaves open.

choices.text: Redundancy: a second phone on each bus
choices.why: That tactic is about a copy taking over on failure, not about stale data.

prompt: The drivers' phones sync at a fixed interval through a ten-hour day. At an interval of 5 minutes, how many times does each phone sync in that day?
In a utility tree, the leaves rated (H, H) are where the ___ is decided.
Joana proposes meeting a need by changing a refund policy, with no code written. In BABOK's terms, is that a solution?

choices.text: Yes: processes, rules and contracts count as solutions
choices.why: Right: business analysis is about change in general, not software.

choices.text: No, a solution in BABOK's sense is a piece of software that gets built
choices.why: BABOK counts processes, policies, contracts and organisational changes as solutions.

choices.text: No, that is a need rather than a solution
choices.why: The need is the problem underneath; the policy change is a way of meeting it.

choices.text: Yes, once the IIBA has approved it
choices.why: No certification body approves a solution.

prompt: The finance director values closing the month faster; Payments values not being paged at night by a job that fails on a malformed file. What does the lesson draw from that?

choices.text: Payments is not a stakeholder in the reconciliation
choices.why: Payments owns the integration the job reads from, and is on the list.

choices.text: The finance director's value wins, being the approver
choices.why: The lesson does not rank them; it notes both are real.

choices.text: Both are value, and they pull different ways
choices.why: Right: asking value to whom is how the core concept model finds the tension.

choices.text: Value belongs in the solution, not among the concepts
choices.why: Value is one of the six core concepts.

prompt: The payment company announced a new settlement file format. How did Carcará know the cost of that change in an afternoon?

choices.text: The finance director estimated it in a workshop
choices.why: An estimate in a room is not how the lesson says it was found.

choices.text: Following the trace from read the settlement file to the requirements and the record behind it
choices.why: Right: it led to two solution requirements, one transition requirement and ADR-0019.

choices.text: By observing Joana match the settlement files for a morning
choices.why: Observation found the hidden routines; this was a change assessed along the trace.

choices.text: The gateway sent an impact report with the announcement
choices.why: The cost came from Carcará's own trace.

prompt: In the RACI for approving the reconciliation requirements, both the finance director and Joana are marked A. What is wrong?

choices.text: Joana should be marked I instead, since she is the one doing the work
choices.why: Doing the work is R; the problem is two As.

choices.text: A RACI table is meant for projects, not for single requirements
choices.why: The lesson uses RACI exactly for who approves requirements.

choices.text: Approval belongs to the architect
choices.why: The approver comes from the RACI, and here that is the finance director.

choices.text: A requirement with two approvers is one nobody owns
choices.why: Right: exactly one A per row is the rule that makes it work.

prompt: A technically excellent reconciliation matches everything the gateway sends and nothing that happens at the counter. Which border failure is it?

choices.text: The analyst designed the solution
choices.why: That failure is a requirement that already decides the architecture, like an SFTP folder at 03:00.

choices.text: Nobody owned the quality numbers
choices.why: That one is about who sets figures like completes by 07:00.

choices.text: The transition requirements were forgotten
choices.why: Those are about moving from the old process to the new one.

choices.text: The architect ignored the business
choices.why: Right: it meets the solution requirements and fails the business one.

prompt: Put BABOK's classes of requirement in the order of the chain, from the one that says why down to the one that says what is built.
items: Business requirements
Stakeholder requirements
Solution requirements
trap: Business goals are met by what stakeholders need, which is met by what the solution does; transition requirements sit beside the chain.

prompt: Which of these are transition requirements for the reconciliation? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Import the 214 known exceptions from Joana's spreadsheet before the first run
choices.why: Right: needed to move from the current state to the future one, and gone after.

choices.text: Run the manual and the automatic match in parallel for one month
choices.why: Right: it ends when the transition does.

choices.text: Train the colleague who covers Joana's holidays
choices.why: Right: not a capability of the new system, and a reason it could fail on its first day.

choices.text: The daily match completes by 07:00 for a day of São João volume
choices.why: That is a non-functional solution requirement, and it lasts as long as the system.

prompt: Match each reconciliation stakeholder to how the stakeholder map says to engage them.
Before Carcará's next programme, a new architect plans to produce each deliverable TOGAF lists, to be safe. What does lesson 8 say about that plan?

choices.text: It is the common failure; the standard asks for the ADM to be tailored
choices.why: Right: the standard says to adapt the ADM, and producing each deliverable because the book lists it is the failure the lesson names.

choices.text: It is what the 10th edition requires before Phase A begins
choices.why: The edition asks for tailoring, not for the full set of deliverables.

choices.text: It suits a company new to enterprise architecture
choices.why: Carcará had not done enterprise architecture before and still tailored in the Preliminary phase.

choices.text: It is the advice of the Series Guide on agile delivery, applied whole
choices.why: The guides on agile practice exist because TOGAF applied whole was criticised as heavy.

prompt: Which of these questions belongs to TOGAF's business architecture domain at Carcará?

choices.text: Which applications hold passengers' personal data?
choices.why: That is a question about applications and data, the information systems architectures.

choices.text: Which capabilities depend on selling to cash customers at the 26 counters?
choices.why: Right: what the organisation does and which capabilities matter is the business layer, the one C4 does not draw.

choices.text: How much traffic do the station internet links carry on the Friday before São João?
choices.why: Networks and links are the technology domain.

choices.text: How are bookings, tickets, trips and payments structured, and who owns each of them?
choices.why: The structure of information is the data domain.

prompt: In Carcará's gap matrix, the receipt print module and the station back office are both eliminated. Why was one elimination accepted as it stood and the other not?

choices.text: The print module cost less to retire than the back office did
choices.why: Cost is not what the check asks; it asks whether a capability was lost without a decision.

choices.text: The station printers were being replaced by tablets in 2026
choices.why: The printers stay and print QR receipts; it is the PCs that tablets replace.

choices.text: Printing moved to the counter mode; the back office hid two capabilities

choices.text: The board voted on the print module in Phase A, but not on the back office

prompt: "The boarding app on Android phones with a local SQLite store, synchronised every 15 minutes." In TOGAF's terms, what is this, and in which phase does it appear?

choices.text: An architecture building block, written in phase B

choices.text: A solution building block, chosen in phase E
choices.why: Right: it says how the capability is provided, with products, and SBBs appear where solutions are chosen.

choices.text: A foundation architecture from the enterprise continuum, kept in phase A
choices.why: Foundation architectures are generic, true of almost any enterprise; this is Carcará's own.

choices.text: A principle, from the Preliminary phase

prompt: TOGAF grades compliance on a scale from irrelevant to non-conformant. What did Carcará take from a compliance review's result?

choices.text: The exact grade, recorded for each of the six steps
choices.why: Carcará skipped the finer grades of compliance, and nobody missed them.

choices.text: Whether the design conforms, and if not, why
choices.why: Right: the lesson says the outcome is what matters, conformant or not and the reason.

choices.text: A score that decides the team's budget for the quarter

choices.text: A ranking of the teams by how conformant they are

prompt: When a station's link drops, Carcará's counter mode switches to an offline sale mode, reconciled later. Up to how many tickets may an agent sell in it?
Which of these are governance mechanisms lesson 8 describes? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An architecture board
choices.why: Right: it approves principles, resolves conflicts and grants exceptions.

choices.text: An architecture contract with a project
choices.why: Right: it states what the project delivers and which architecture it conforms to.

choices.text: A dispensation with an end date
choices.why: Right: a recorded, time-limited exception granted by the board.

choices.text: The gap analysis matrix
choices.why: That is the technique of phases B to D for finding the work, not a governance mechanism.

prompt: A vendor sells Carcará's directors on its ticket validators, and Tainá is asked to write the reasons afterwards. How does that decision look in IAF's grid?

choices.text: Floating: a physical choice with nothing above it in its column
choices.why: Right: starting at with what? and writing the reasons backwards is the failure IAF's ordering makes visible.

choices.text: Sound: product choices come first and the levels above follow
choices.why: IAF's rule is the reverse: each level is justified by the one above it.

choices.text: Complete, since the vendor's pitch fills the contextual level of the grid
choices.why: A sales pitch is not the organisation's drivers, goals or principles.

choices.text: Misplaced: products belong to the conceptual level of each column
choices.why: The conceptual level names services and information with no product; products are physical.

prompt: IAF's grid has sixteen cells plus two cross-cutting concerns. How much of it did Carcará's digital boarding programme fill?

choices.text: Each of the sixteen cells, since an empty cell is a gap in the design
choices.why: IAF does not ask for the whole grid; most cells were left as references to what existed.

choices.text: The cells the change touched, to the depth the decisions needed
choices.why: Right: four levels of information systems and technology, the top two of business and information, and references for the rest.

choices.text: The physical row, since the products were what changed
choices.why: The programme filled the contextual and conceptual levels too, where the reasons live.

choices.text: The contextual row, leaving the rest to each project
choices.why: Information systems and technology were filled down to the physical level.

prompt: In Carcará's ArchiMate view, ticketing accesses the data object booking. To which of ArchiMate's aspects does the booking belong?

choices.text: Active structure
choices.why: Active structure is who or what does something: an actor, a component, a node.

choices.text: Behaviour
choices.why: Behaviour is what is done: a process, a function, a service.

choices.text: Passive structure
choices.why: Right: a data object is what a behaviour is done to.

choices.text: Motivation layer
choices.why: Motivation covers goals, principles and requirements, and it is not one of the three aspects.

prompt: Someone proposes that Carcará adopt DoDAF or NAF for its own architecture. What follows from lesson 9?

choices.text: NAF, because it replaced MODAF and is the newer of the two
choices.why: Being newer does not give Carcará the problem these frameworks solve.

choices.text: DoDAF, because its viewpoints cover capability and services
choices.why: The viewpoints exist so many contractors' descriptions fit together, which Carcará does not need.

choices.text: Neither: the problem they solve is absent here
choices.why: Right: they exist so that many organisations or suppliers produce descriptions that combine, and a company of Carcará's size gains nothing from that weight.

choices.text: Both together, one for operations and one for systems
choices.why: Two frameworks of the same weight double the problem rather than solving one.

prompt: Gartner's approach to enterprise architecture is a body of advice rather than a published framework. What does it emphasise, by lesson 9?

choices.text: A certified method with a published standard
choices.why: That describes TOGAF, not an analyst firm's advice.

choices.text: Business outcomes, modelling what helps decide
choices.why: Right: start from what the business is trying to achieve and measure architecture by the decisions it improves.

choices.text: Reference models shared across government agencies
choices.why: That is FEAF's contribution.

choices.text: One notation across business, application and technology layers
choices.why: That is ArchiMate.

prompt: Match each item of Carcará's digital boarding to its IAF aspect area.

pairs.left: What a ticket means to Sales and to Finance
Ticketing, the boarding app and the counter mode
Drivers' phones, station tablets and links
The counter sale with a QR receipt

prompt: ArchiMate is to enterprise architecture what ___ is to software design.
The operations room has a wall map of Carcará's 26 stations and 140 routes, which nobody counted as architecture. Which Zachman cell does it fill?

choices.text: Where, for the engineer
choices.why: Where for the engineer is the deployment diagram, drawn in technical terms.

choices.text: Where, for business management
choices.why: Right: the stations and routes as the business sees them, the cell the course left empty.

choices.text: What, for the executive
choices.why: What for the executive lists the things of interest, such as passengers and buses.

choices.text: How, for the architect
choices.why: How for the architect is a logical process, like the activity diagram.

prompt: A team trained on 1980s information systems insists Carcará's What column be modelled before the others. What does Zachman's grid say?

choices.text: It agrees, since data is the foundation of the other columns
choices.why: Treating data as primary is a choice the grid does not make for you.

choices.text: It puts Why first, so the team has the order backwards
choices.why: The grid has no starting cell and puts no column ahead of another.

choices.text: The columns have no order; that priority is the team's choice
choices.why: Right: it is one of the two rules of the grid, and the grid leaves such a priority to whoever uses it.

choices.text: It follows the rows, so the executive's What comes first
choices.why: Rows are audiences, not steps; the grid is an ontology with no order of production.

prompt: A team applies TOGAF in full to one small service and drowns in paperwork. Which of lesson 10's three sorting questions would have warned them?

choices.text: Is it a method, a taxonomy, a notation or a template?
choices.why: TOGAF is a method either way; the mistake was the size of what it was applied to.

choices.text: What scale is the framework meant for?
choices.why: Right: an enterprise framework applied to one service produces paperwork, as the lesson warns.

choices.text: What is its one central idea?
choices.why: Knowing the ADM cycle's idea does not tell the team it is too big for one service.

choices.text: Who certifies it, and at what level?
choices.why: Certification is not one of the three questions.

prompt: You are aiming at a first architect role in a product company. What does lesson 10 say will serve you better than any certificate?

choices.text: TOGAF Foundation, then Practitioner
choices.why: Those are what corporate job descriptions name, as desirable rather than required.

choices.text: A list of the frameworks you have read about
choices.why: The names get the CV read; the habits get the job.

choices.text: C4 and decision records, done well
choices.why: Right: in a product company, C4 and decision records done well serve better than a certificate.

choices.text: An ArchiMate certification next to the IIBA's
choices.why: Certifications appear as desirable on corporate roles; the lesson points product companies elsewhere.

prompt: Where in the Zachman grid does the whole of C4 sit, by lesson 10?

choices.text: Roughly rows 3 and 4, zooming inside them
choices.why: Right: C4's levels zoom within the architect's and engineer's rows, for technical readers.

choices.text: Rows 1 to 4, one row per C4 level
choices.why: C4's levels are one kind of description at different magnifications, not four audiences.

choices.text: Row 2, beside the BPMN models
choices.why: Row 2 is the business manager's process model, a different kind of thing from C4.

choices.text: Row 6, since it describes the running system
choices.why: Row 6 is the running thing itself, not a description of it.

prompt: In what year did John Zachman first publish his framework, in an IBM journal article?
Which of these are rules of the Zachman grid stated in lesson 10? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Each cell is primitive
choices.why: Right: a model in a cell answers one question for one audience.

choices.text: The columns have no order
choices.why: Right: what is not more important than why.

choices.text: Each row adds detail to the one above
choices.why: That is the most common misreading; rows are audiences.

choices.text: Work starts at Why for the executive
choices.why: There is no starting cell; a method would have one, and the grid is not a method.

prompt: Carcará's ticketing document in arc42 runs to eleven pages. Which part is the longest, and why?

choices.text: Part 8, as newcomers break the offline and idempotency rules

choices.text: Part 5, because each component is listed in it
choices.why: The building block view is there, but it is not the longest at Carcará.

prompt: "Why boarding works offline" is one of Carcará's pages. In Diátaxis terms, what kind is it, and what does it carry to stay honest?

choices.text: A how-to guide, with an owner who answers when a step breaks
choices.why: A how-to guide helps someone reach a goal; this page explains a reason.

choices.text: Explanation, with the date it was written
choices.why: Right: explanation ages best, and a reason is true as of the moment it was written.

choices.text: Reference, generated from the deployment configuration
choices.why: Reference is what is looked up, like the container catalogue; this page is studied.

choices.text: A tutorial, tested by a newcomer on day one
choices.why: A tutorial is a guided exercise for somebody learning by doing.

prompt: A page describing the nightly Frota export is out of date, and its owner has no time this month. By Carcará's three questions, what happens to it?

choices.text: It is archived with a banner, since its content is out of date and unowned
choices.why: Archiving is for pages that explain a past state, not for the one description of something current.

choices.text: It is deleted, and version control keeps its history for anybody who asks
choices.why: Deleting the one description of the export loses knowledge nobody else wrote down.

choices.text: It is kept and fixed first, as the one place that job is described
choices.why: Right: the third question keeps the sole copy of something and fixes it first, whatever its state.

choices.text: It is replaced by a tombstone pointing at the code
choices.why: A tombstone is for a page linked from many places whose content has a replacement.

prompt: Carcará's documentation numbers improved a great deal in one quarter. Where did most of the improvement come from?

choices.text: Rewriting the 109 pages nobody had edited

choices.text: A new wiki tool
choices.why: The pages stayed in the repository as plain text.

choices.text: Doubling the pages to cover the empty Zachman cells
choices.why: The set shrank; it did not grow.

prompt: Carcará uses C4, decision records and arc42 together. How do the three fit, by lesson 11?

choices.text: The decision records are copied into arc42's part 4, one per page

choices.text: C4 diagrams fill parts 3, 5 and 7; part 9 links to the records' index
choices.why: Right: arc42 gives the headings that hold the C4 diagrams and points to the decision log.

choices.text: C4 replaces arc42's sections, so the template is left out
choices.why: The lesson uses arc42 as the container that holds the C4 diagrams.

choices.text: arc42 replaces the records, as part 9 is the log
choices.why: Part 9 is the decision log or links to it; the records remain their own files.

prompt: After one quarter, 57 of Carcará's 64 surviving pages had been verified in the past 12 months. How many had not?

choices.text: A binary file that changed

choices.why: Right: a readable diff, which a reviewer reads and questions line by line.

choices.text: The rendered picture before and after the change, side by side

choices.text: A list of the boxes whose position moved in the automatic layout

prompt: You run Structurizr's validate on workspace.dsl and it prints nothing. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The model is sound

choices.text: Its views were exported to Mermaid

prompt: A team keeps its flows as Mermaid blocks inside README files on GitHub. What does that cost them, by lesson 12?

choices.text: GitHub draws the blocks as plain code

choices.why: Right: the site draws them, and a broken block is caught when the pipeline renders it too.

choices.text: The diagram changes in a different pull request from the code it describes
choices.why: The block sits in the README and changes in the same pull request as the code.

choices.text: Each reader needs Node.js installed to see them
choices.why: Readers see them drawn by the site; the renderer is for files and pipelines.

prompt: PlantUML's -syntax check on broken.puml answered ERROR, then 5. What does the 5 count?

prompt: A diagram renders on a developer's laptop and fails in CI, with the same source. Which pipeline habit from lesson 12 was missed?

choices.text: Pinning the tool versions the team uses
choices.why: Right: without pinned versions, a diagram that renders on a laptop fails in CI, or the reverse.

choices.text: Publishing the rendered SVGs to the site
choices.why: Publishing keeps readers on current pictures; it does not make two renders agree.

choices.text: Using -syntax instead of -checkonly
choices.why: -checkonly is the stricter of the two, and the switch would not explain a version mismatch.

choices.text: Validating the model as well as the syntax
choices.why: That catches missing elements and duplicate names, not a difference between machines.

prompt: Put the steps of producing C4 diagrams from Carcará's Structurizr model in the order lesson 12 runs them.

Render a Mermaid file to SVG with mmdc

prompt: Carcará's workspace.dsl asks for views in its views block. How many views does it define?
In a review of Carcará's purchase path, an engineer says: "I would have used Kafka." What does lesson 13 make of comments like that?

choices.text: A risk, to be ranked by likelihood and impact with the others
choices.why: A risk ties a decision to a scenario that could go unmet; this ties to no scenario.

choices.text: Taste, until it is put as a question about a scenario
choices.why: Right: with quality scenarios in hand, a comment becomes a question such as whether QS-01 is met and how anybody knows.

choices.text: A trade-off point, owned by whoever proposed it
choices.why: A trade-off point is a property two qualities depend on in opposite directions.

choices.text: A finding, ready for the team tracker
choices.why: A finding names a scenario, a cause, evidence and a next step.

prompt: The queue in front of purchases is sized for 2,500 a minute; last year's peak was 2,300, and one more route would exceed it. What is that in ATAM's terms?

choices.text: A non-risk, since today's peak fits under the limit
choices.why: A non-risk is judged sound for its scenarios; this one is a route away from failing.

choices.text: A risk theme
choices.why: A theme is a pattern several risks share; this is a single risk.

choices.text: A risk: a decision that could leave a scenario unmet
choices.why: Right: it is the lesson's own example of a risk.

choices.text: A trade-off point between capacity and cost
choices.why: The lesson's trade-off point is the sync interval, where two qualities pull apart.

prompt: ATAM's step 7 brings operations, support, finance and others into the review. Which of lesson 13's ways a review goes wrong does it exist to prevent?

choices.text: The rubber stamp
choices.why: The rubber stamp is cured by timing, reviewing before the commitment.

choices.text: Bikeshedding over names
choices.why: Bikeshedding is cured by the utility tree setting the agenda.

choices.text: The missing voice
choices.why: Right: without step 7 the scenarios are the architects' own, and Carcará's most important one came from a station agent.

choices.text: The gate run by outsiders
choices.why: The gate is cured by answers predictable from written principles.

prompt: Carcará's station-link risk theme was the biggest finding before São João. Where did it come from?

choices.text: A checklist question about the links
choices.why: The lesson says the theme did not come from a checklist question.

choices.text: The architects' first pass over the utility tree and its scenarios
choices.why: The architects' own scenarios missed it; the station side came in later.

choices.text: Following three different not-sure answers until they met
choices.why: Right: the questions are where the review starts, and each not sure is a thread to pull.

choices.text: An incident in the year before the review, at a coastal station
choices.why: The lesson describes no incident behind it; it came out of the review itself.

choices.text: A backup slide for the directors

prompt: On Wednesday, Otávio and the product managers decide what is built before the peak. What did Tainá show them besides the system context?

choices.text: The fourteen risks, one per slide

prompt: The same review went to the directors on Monday and the engineers on Thursday. How did the engineers' version of the findings differ?

choices.text: The theme on one slide, then the risks their own teams owned
choices.why: Right: the same review at two altitudes, with each finding's scenario and owner for the engineers.

choices.text: The same slides as Monday, with the protocols added to each line

prompt: Which sentence does lesson 14 hold up as stronger, in front of the directors, than a confident one?

choices.why: Right: it tells the directors exactly where their money buys certainty.

choices.text: Fourteen risks were found and are under control
choices.why: The directors needed the theme and its decision, not a count.

prompt: Tainá told the room: "the passenger app, the payments and the boarding app are not touched." What did that sentence achieve at Carcará?

choices.text: It closed the open questions in the pack

prompt: A container diagram of fifteen boxes needs to appear in the deck for the engineers. What does lesson 14 advise?
